questions.title: Wernicke's disease and beriberi reversed by which vitamin
questions.question: Both Wernicke's disease and beriberi can be reversed by administering:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency produces a different clinical picture (convulsions via impaired GABA synthesis); it does not reverse Wernicke's disease or beriberi.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vitamin B12 deficiency produces megaloblastic anaemia and subacute combined degeneration, an unrelated clinical picture; it does not reverse Wernicke's disease or beriberi.
explanations.C: Correct. Thiamine (vitamin B1), as its coenzyme thiamine pyrophosphate, is required for oxidative decarboxylation reactions central to glucose metabolism, and its deficiency underlies both Wernicke's disease (a CNS presentation) and beriberi (a cardiovascular/peripheral-nerve presentation). Administering thiamine reverses both, since both trace back to the same underlying deficiency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Retinol (vitamin A) deficiency produces night blindness and xerophthalmia; it does not reverse Wernicke's disease or beriberi.

questions.learning_objective: State that thiamine administration reverses both Wernicke's disease and beriberi.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Thiamin", p12

questions.title: Disease caused by vitamin B1 deficiency
questions.question: Vitamin B1 deficiency causes:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rickets is the childhood presentation of vitamin D deficiency, affecting bone mineralisation, not vitamin B1 deficiency.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Nyctalopia (night blindness) is caused by vitamin A deficiency, not vitamin B1 deficiency.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pellagra is caused by niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency, not vitamin B1 deficiency, though both are B-vitamin deficiencies.
explanations.D: Correct. Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency causes beriberi. Its thiamine pyrophosphate-dependent oxidative decarboxylation deficit underlies both beriberi's cardiovascular (wet beriberi) and peripheral-nerve (dry beriberi) presentations.

questions.title: Raised blood pyruvic and lactic acid from vitamin deficiency
questions.question: Concentration of pyruvic acid and lactic acid in blood is increased due to deficiency of the vitamin:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Riboflavin deficiency produces glossitis and angular stomatitis, not a rise in blood pyruvate and lactate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Niacin deficiency produces pellagra, not the pyruvate/lactate accumulation this question describes.
explanations.C: Correct. Thiamine pyrophosphate is the coenzyme the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex requires to oxidatively decarboxylate pyruvate into acetyl-CoA. When thiamine is deficient, this step is blocked, so pyruvate (and the lactate it is reduced to) accumulates in the blood.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pantothenic acid deficiency is rare and is not characteristically associated with raised blood pyruvate and lactate.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Thiamin", p13

questions.title: Reaction run by thiamine coenzyme TPP
questions.question: Vitamin B1 coenzyme (thiamine pyrophosphate, TPP) is involved in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Transamination is run by pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6's coenzyme), not thiamine pyrophosphate.
explanations.B: Correct. Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is the coenzyme for oxidative decarboxylation reactions. Pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and the branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex all require it, alongside its separate role in transketolase.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hydroxylation reactions typically require vitamin C (as in collagen synthesis) or other specific cofactors, not thiamine pyrophosphate.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Carboxylation reactions typically require biotin as their coenzyme, not thiamine pyrophosphate.

questions.title: Vitamin deficiency causing glossitis
questions.question: Glossitis is found in the deficiency of the vitamin:

explanations.A: Correct. Riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency characteristically causes glossitis (inflammation of the tongue) alongside angular stomatitis and corneal vascularisation. These mucocutaneous signs reflect riboflavin's role, as FAD and FMN, in the oxidation-reduction reactions of rapidly turning-over epithelial tissue.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Thiamin deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke's disease, not glossitis as its characteristic mucocutaneous sign.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pyridoxine deficiency is linked to convulsions (via impaired GABA synthesis), not glossitis as its characteristic sign.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nicotinic acid (niacin) deficiency causes pellagra's dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia triad, not glossitis specifically as the characteristic finding this question tests.

questions.learning_objective: State that riboflavin deficiency causes glossitis.

questions.title: Vitamin deficiency causing corneal vascularisation
questions.question: Corneal vascularisation is found in deficiency of the vitamin:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid) deficiency is rare and is not characteristically linked to corneal vascularisation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency is linked to convulsions, not corneal vascularisation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vitamin B1 (thiamin) deficiency causes beriberi, not corneal vascularisation.
explanations.D: Correct. Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) deficiency characteristically causes corneal vascularisation, alongside glossitis and angular stomatitis. New blood vessels grow in from the limbus into the normally avascular cornea, a change that can be seen directly on examination.

questions.title: The pellagra preventive factor
questions.question: The pellagra preventive factor is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pyridoxine deficiency is linked to convulsions, not pellagra; it is not the pellagra-preventive factor.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Riboflavin deficiency causes glossitis and corneal vascularisation, not pellagra; it is not the pellagra-preventive factor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pantothenic acid is the vitamin of coenzyme A; it is not the pellagra-preventive factor.
explanations.D: Correct. Niacin (nicotinic acid, vitamin B3) is the pellagra-preventive factor -- its deficiency is the direct cause of pellagra, whose classic triad is dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia. The body can also synthesise niacin endogenously from tryptophan, though inefficiently, which is why a tryptophan-poor diet compounds the risk.

questions.learning_objective: Identify niacin as the pellagra-preventive factor.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Niacin", p14

questions.title: Deficiency that causes pellagra
questions.question: Pellagra is caused due to the deficiency of:

explanations.A: Correct. Pellagra is caused by niacin (nicotinic acid) deficiency, presenting with its classic triad of dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia. explanations.C: Incorrect. Pantothenic acid deficiency is rare and does not cause pellagra.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Thiamin deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke's disease, not pellagra.

questions.title: Amino acid niacin is synthesized from
questions.question: Niacin is synthesized in the body from:

explanations.A: Correct. The body can synthesise niacin endogenously from the essential amino acid tryptophan, though inefficiently. About 60 mg of tryptophan is needed to produce 1 mg of niacin, which is why diets low in both tryptophan and niacin, as in populations dependent on corn, predispose to pellagra. This dual dependence is also why niacin is sometimes classed as a conditionally essential nutrient rather than a strict vitamin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glutamate is not the amino acid precursor of niacin; it is instead the substrate for glutamate decarboxylase in a separate, PLP-dependent pathway producing GABA.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Aspartate is not the amino acid precursor of niacin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tyrosine is not the amino acid precursor of niacin; it is instead the precursor of catecholamines and thyroid hormone.

questions.learning_objective: State that niacin can be synthesised in the body from tryptophan.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Tryptophan", p15

questions.title: Amino acid deficient in corn protein
questions.question: The proteins present in corn are deficient in:

explanations.A: Correct. Corn (maize) protein is characteristically deficient in tryptophan, as well as lysine. This is exactly why populations whose diet depends heavily on corn are predisposed to pellagra, since tryptophan is both an essential amino acid in its own right and the body's only endogenous precursor for niacin synthesis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Threonine is not the amino acid corn protein is characteristically noted as deficient in, in the context of this pellagra-related teaching point.
explanations.C: Incorrect. While corn protein is also low in lysine, the deficiency this question and its printed key specifically test is tryptophan, given its direct link to niacin synthesis and pellagra.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tyrosine is not the amino acid corn protein is characteristically noted as deficient in.

questions.title: Tryptophan needed to produce 1 mg niacin
questions.question: In the body, 1 mg of niacin can be produced from:

explanations.A: Correct. The body's conversion of tryptophan to niacin is inefficient. About 60 mg of dietary tryptophan is required to yield 1 mg of niacin, which is why a tryptophan-poor diet compounds a niacin-poor one in populations at risk of pellagra. Corn-dependent diets are the classic example, since corn protein is itself deficient in tryptophan.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pantothenic acid is not a precursor of niacin at all; niacin's amino-acid precursor is tryptophan, not pantothenic acid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pyridoxine is not a precursor of niacin; it is a separate B-vitamin with its own distinct coenzyme role (transamination).
explanations.D: Incorrect. The correct ratio is 60 mg of tryptophan per 1 mg of niacin, not 30 mg -- this option understates the amount of tryptophan actually required.

questions.learning_objective: State that about 60 mg of tryptophan is required to produce 1 mg of niacin in the body.

questions.title: Population at risk of pellagra by staple food
questions.question: Pellagra occurs in populations dependent on:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Wheat-dependent diets are not the classic risk population for pellagra described in this teaching point.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rice-dependent diets are more classically linked to beriberi (thiamine deficiency) than to pellagra.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Milk is not deficient in tryptophan or niacin in the way corn is, and milk-dependent diets are not the classic pellagra risk population.
explanations.D: Correct. Populations whose staple diet is corn (maize) are at classic risk of pellagra. Corn protein is deficient in tryptophan, the body's only endogenous precursor for niacin, which compounds a diet already low in niacin itself. About 60 mg of tryptophan is normally needed to yield 1 mg of niacin, so this dietary gap is not easily made up.

questions.title: Precursor of coenzyme A
questions.question: The precursor of coenzyme A (CoA) is:

explanations.A: Correct. Pantothenic acid (as pantothenate) is the vitamin precursor of coenzyme A. Coenzyme A is the universal acyl-group carrier central to fatty acid metabolism, the citric acid cycle and many other acyl-transfer reactions, so a pantothenate shortfall would touch a very wide range of pathways at once.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pyridoxamine is a form of vitamin B6, unrelated to coenzyme A's biosynthesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Riboflavin is the precursor of FAD and FMN, hydrogen-carrying coenzymes, not of coenzyme A.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Thiamin is the precursor of thiamine pyrophosphate, an oxidative-decarboxylation coenzyme, not of coenzyme A.

questions.learning_objective: State that pantothenate is the vitamin precursor of coenzyme A.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Pantothenate", p16

questions.title: Vitamin that is a coenzyme of carboxylase enzymes
questions.question: Biotin is a coenzyme of the enzyme class:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Deaminases remove amino groups without carbon dioxide transfer; biotin is not the coenzyme this enzyme class requires.
explanations.B: Correct. Biotin is the coenzyme carboxylase enzymes require. It functions as a mobile carrier of carbon dioxide (as carboxybiotin) that is transferred onto the substrate. Pyruvate carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase are two of the best-known examples of enzymes that depend on it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Decarboxylases remove, rather than add, a carboxyl group, and most (such as glutamate decarboxylase) require pyridoxal phosphate, not biotin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hydroxylases add a hydroxyl group and typically require different cofactors (such as vitamin C for prolyl hydroxylase); biotin is not their characteristic coenzyme.

questions.learning_objective: State that biotin is the coenzyme carboxylase enzymes require.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Carboxylase", p18

questions.title: Coenzyme for pyruvate to oxaloacetate conversion
questions.question: The coenzyme required for conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate is:

explanations.A: Correct. Pyruvate carboxylase, the mitochondrial enzyme that carboxylates pyruvate to oxaloacetate, requires biotin as its coenzyme (alongside ATP and magnesium). Acetyl-CoA is the enzyme's allosteric activator, which is how a cell already rich in acetyl-CoA ensures itself the oxaloacetate citrate synthase needs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. FAD is the coenzyme for flavin-dependent oxidation-reduction reactions (such as succinate dehydrogenase), not for pyruvate carboxylase's carboxylation reaction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate) is the coenzyme for pyruvate dehydrogenase's oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA -- a different reaction (and different fate for pyruvate) from the carboxylation this question asks about.
explanations.D: Incorrect. NAD is a hydrogen-carrying coenzyme used in many oxidation-reduction reactions, not the coenzyme for pyruvate carboxylase's carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate.

questions.learning_objective: State that biotin is the coenzyme pyruvate carboxylase requires to convert pyruvate to oxaloacetate.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Biotin", p18

questions.title: Vitamin deficiency from raw egg consumption
questions.question: Consumption of raw eggs can cause deficiency of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Raw eggs are not characteristically linked to thiamin deficiency.
explanations.B: Correct. Raw egg white contains avidin, a protein that binds biotin with extremely high affinity, preventing its intestinal absorption. Consuming large quantities of raw egg white over time can therefore cause biotin deficiency (cooking denatures avidin and removes this risk).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Raw eggs are not characteristically linked to riboflavin deficiency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Raw eggs are not characteristically linked to pantothenic acid deficiency.

questions.title: Cofactor for acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA conversion
questions.question: The cofactor required for the conversion of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. FAD is a hydrogen-carrying coenzyme for oxidation-reduction reactions, not the cofactor acetyl-CoA carboxylase requires.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acyl carrier protein (ACP) carries the growing fatty acid chain during fatty acid synthase's later steps, but it is not the cofactor for the carboxylation step this question asks about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. NAD is a hydrogen-carrying coenzyme, not the cofactor for acetyl-CoA carboxylase's carboxylation reaction.
explanations.D: Correct. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is the key regulatory enzyme of fatty acid synthesis (lipogenesis). It requires biotin as its cofactor to carboxylate acetyl-CoA into malonyl-CoA, the committed first step of the pathway. Every major hormonal control signal over lipogenesis converges on regulating this one enzyme.

questions.learning_objective: State that biotin is the cofactor acetyl-CoA carboxylase requires to convert acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Biotin", p19

questions.title: Vitamins required to methylate homocysteine to methionine
questions.question: Both folic acid and methyl cobalamin (vitamin B12) are required in:

options.A: Conversion of pyridoxal phosphate to pyridoxamine phosphate

explanations.A: Incorrect. Interconverting pyridoxal phosphate and pyridoxamine phosphate is part of vitamin B6's own coenzyme cycling, not a reaction that needs folate and B12 together.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Deamination of serine does not require both folate and B12 together as its coenzymes.
explanations.C: Correct. Methionine synthase transfers a methyl group from methyltetrahydrofolate (the folate coenzyme) to homocysteine, regenerating methionine, and requires methylcobalamin (the B12 coenzyme) as an intermediate methyl carrier in the reaction cycle. Both vitamins are therefore required together for this specific methylation step.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Deamination of threonine does not require both folate and B12 together as its coenzymes.

questions.learning_objective: State that folate and methylcobalamin are both required for methylation of homocysteine to methionine.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Methylation of homocystein to methionine", p20

questions.title: Group transferred by folate as a coenzyme
questions.question: Folate as a coenzyme is involved in the transfer and utilization of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Transferring a hydroxyl group is not folate's coenzyme role; that kind of transfer is instead associated with hydroxylation reactions using different cofactors.
explanations.B: Correct. Folate, as tetrahydrofolate, is the coenzyme that carries and transfers single-carbon (one-carbon) units. These units can be carried in several oxidation states -- methyl, methylene, formyl and others -- and are used across a wide range of biosynthetic reactions, including purine and thymidylate synthesis and the methylation of homocysteine to methionine. This is exactly why folate deficiency, by starving DNA synthesis of these one-carbon units, produces megaloblastic anaemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transferring an amido group is not folate's characteristic coenzyme role.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Transferring an amino group (transamination) is pyridoxal phosphate's role, not folate's.

questions.learning_objective: State that folate's coenzyme role is to transfer single-carbon moieties.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Single carbon moiety", p21

questions.title: Anaemia caused by folate deficiency
questions.question: Folate deficiency causes:

explanations.A: Correct. Folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis, via its role in purine and thymidylate synthesis. This produces megaloblastic anaemia -- large, immature red cell precursors -- the same blood picture vitamin B12 deficiency produces. The two are distinguished by the methylmalonate level, which is raised in B12 deficiency but normal in folate deficiency.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Microcytic anaemia (small red cells) is characteristic of iron deficiency or thalassaemia, not folate deficiency, which produces macrocytic, megaloblastic cells instead.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Iron deficiency anaemia is a distinct entity caused by iron lack, not folate deficiency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Haemolytic anaemia results from increased red cell destruction, a different mechanism from folate deficiency's DNA-synthesis defect.

questions.learning_objective: State that folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Megaloblastic anemia", p21

questions.title: Symptoms of pellagra
questions.question: Symptoms of pellagra are:

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own. Diarrhoea and dermatitis are two of pellagra's classic three features, but the classic description is a triad, not just these two.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own. Dermatitis and diarrhoea are two of the three, but again not the complete classic triad.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own. Dermatitis and dementia are two of the three, but again not the complete classic triad.
explanations.D: Correct. Pellagra, caused by niacin deficiency, is classically described by its "three Ds": diarrhoea, dermatitis and dementia. The dermatitis characteristically appears in sun-exposed areas, and untreated pellagra can progress to death, giving rise to the mnemonic "the three Ds and death". All three features together, not any two alone, make up the disease's classic clinical description.

questions.learning_objective: State pellagra's classic triad of diarrhoea, dermatitis and dementia.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Diarrhea, dermatitis and dementia", p25

questions.title: The sulphur-containing B vitamin
questions.question: The sulphur-containing vitamin among the following B-vitamins is:

explanations.A: Correct. Thiamine (vitamin B1) is the sulphur-containing B vitamin among the options listed -- its thiazole ring carries a sulphur atom, which is in fact the origin of the name "thiamine" (from the Greek/chemical root "thio-", meaning sulphur). This is a distinct, structural fact from thiamine's better-known coenzyme role (as thiamine pyrophosphate) in oxidative decarboxylation reactions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Riboflavin (vitamin B2) does not carry a sulphur atom in its structure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Niacin (vitamin B3) does not carry a sulphur atom in its structure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) does not carry a sulphur atom in its structure.

questions.title: Glucose transporter defect in insulin-resistant type 2 diabetes
questions.question: A 47-year-old obese man complains of having to get out of bed three times a night to urinate (polyuria), being constantly thirsty (polydipsia), and eating more often (polyphagia). The patient is diagnosed with insulin resistant diabetes mellitus (type 2). If the patient's symptoms are due to a problem at the level of the glucose transporter, which one of the tissues indicated below will be most affected?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Liver glucose uptake is mediated by GLUT-2, a high-Km, insulin-independent transporter; it is not the transporter defective in insulin-resistant states.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Red blood cells take up glucose via GLUT-1, an insulin-independent transporter providing basal glucose supply; it is not affected by insulin resistance.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Intestinal glucose absorption is largely via SGLT-1, a sodium-coupled, insulin-independent transporter; it is not the transporter this insulin-resistance question targets.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Brain glucose uptake occurs mainly via GLUT-1 and GLUT-3, both insulin-independent transporters that guarantee the brain's glucose supply regardless of insulin status.
explanations.E: Correct. GLUT-4 is the only insulin-dependent glucose transporter, expressed principally in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, where insulin signalling normally recruits GLUT-4 to the cell surface to allow glucose uptake. In insulin-resistant type 2 diabetes, this insulin-triggered GLUT-4 recruitment fails, so muscle (and fat) tissue is specifically starved of glucose uptake despite high circulating glucose, which is exactly the tissue-level defect underlying this patient's presentation. This is why skeletal muscle, the largest insulin-dependent glucose sink in the body, is the tissue most affected when the GLUT-4 pathway itself is the problem.

questions.learning_objective: Identify skeletal muscle as the tissue most affected by a GLUT-4 defect in insulin-resistant type 2 diabetes.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Muscle", p39-40

questions.title: Protein that traps the PET glucose tracer in a cell
questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with breast cancer presents with confusion, headaches, and persistent nausea. To evaluate for metastases to the brain, the oncologist orders a positron emission tomography (PET) scan, which covalently links a radioactive isotope to glucose and reveals highly active areas in the body (e.g., a tumor). Which of the following proteins enables the tracer to remain in the cell?

explanations.A: Incorrect. PFK-1 acts later in glycolysis, on fructose-6-phosphate; it is not the enzyme responsible for the first, trapping phosphorylation of the glucose tracer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Insulin regulates glucose uptake into insulin-dependent tissues via GLUT-4 recruitment, but it is not itself the protein that chemically traps the glucose tracer inside a cell once taken up.
explanations.C: Incorrect. GLUT-1 gets glucose (and the PET tracer) into the cell, but transport alone does not trap it there; without phosphorylation the tracer could simply diffuse back out.
explanations.D: Correct. Once glucose (or its PET tracer analogue, fluorodeoxyglucose) enters a cell, hexokinase immediately phosphorylates it to glucose-6-phosphate. This phosphorylated form cannot cross the cell membrane and, being a poor substrate for the next glycolytic enzyme in the tracer's modified form, accumulates inside the cell -- a phenomenon called metabolic trapping. This is exactly the mechanism that lets a PET scan visualise tissue with high glucose uptake and phosphorylation activity, such as a rapidly growing tumour, as a signal that accumulates rather than washing back out.
explanations.E: Incorrect. GLUT-4 is the insulin-dependent glucose transporter of muscle and fat; it moves glucose into the cell but, like GLUT-1, does not itself trap it there.

questions.learning_objective: Explain PET tracer trapping in a cell through hexokinase-mediated phosphorylation to glucose-6-phosphate.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Hexokinase", p40-41

questions.title: Correct statement on muscle lactate formation during exercise
questions.question: Which one of the following statements is correct concerning the formation of muscle lactate during exercise?

options.A: Lactate formation is less likely to be found in the eye, testes and RBCs than in other tissues
options.B: Lactate formation occurs when the NADH/NAD+ ratio is high
options.C: The liver preferentially converts lactate into carbon dioxide and water
options.D: The intracellular pH is typically increased when lactate is produced
options.E: The heart preferentially converts lactate into glucose

explanations.A: Incorrect. The eye, testes and red blood cells are among the tissues that rely heavily on anaerobic glycolysis and lactate production (RBCs have no mitochondria at all), so lactate formation is, if anything, more, not less, prominent in them compared with many other tissues.
explanations.B: Correct. Anaerobic glycolysis reduces pyruvate to lactate specifically to regenerate the NAD+ that glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase needs to keep glycolysis running when oxidative NADH reoxidation (via the respiratory chain) cannot keep pace, as happens during vigorous exercise. A high, rather than low, NADH/NAD+ ratio is exactly the signal that drives this lactate dehydrogenase reaction toward lactate, since mass action pushes the reaction to consume the excess NADH and regenerate NAD+. This NAD+-regeneration purpose, not lactate itself, is the real point of the reaction -- lactate is a byproduct of keeping glycolysis's redox balance sustainable, not an end in itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The liver preferentially converts lactate back into glucose via gluconeogenesis (the Cori cycle), not into carbon dioxide and water.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lactate production typically decreases, not increases, intracellular pH, since it is accompanied by proton release, contributing to the acidosis of vigorous exercise.
explanations.E: Incorrect. It is the liver, not the heart, that preferentially converts lactate back into glucose; the heart instead tends to take up and oxidise lactate as a fuel.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that a high NADH/NAD+ ratio drives lactate formation during anaerobic exercise, to regenerate NAD+ for glycolysis.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Lactate formation occurs when the NADH/ NAD+ ratio is high", p41-42

questions.title: Significant characteristic of glucokinase in MODY2
questions.question: An 8-year-old girl presents with polydipsia, polyuria, and fatigue. A urinalysis is significant for glucose. To differentiate between type 1 diabetes mellitus and maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY), an assay is run to identify one of the six proteins responsible for MODY. Results reveal a missense mutation in exon 7 of the glucokinase gene establishing MODY2. Which of the following is a significant characteristic of glucokinase?

options.A: It is expressed only in muscle
options.B: The Km is above the fasting concentration of glucose in the blood
options.C: Its activity is stimulated in response to fructose 2,6-bisphosphate
options.D: Its activity is inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate
options.E: It is expressed in many tissues

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glucokinase is expressed specifically in liver and pancreatic beta cells, not in muscle, which instead relies on the low-Km hexokinase.
explanations.B: Correct. Glucokinase has a high Km for glucose, above the normal fasting blood glucose concentration, in contrast to hexokinase's much lower Km. This means glucokinase's activity rises with blood glucose across the normal physiological range rather than saturating at fasting levels, which is exactly what makes it suited to its role as the liver's and pancreatic beta cell's glucose sensor -- for instance, driving glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in the beta cell as glucose rises after a meal. A glucokinase mutation, as in MODY2, disturbs this glucose-sensing function and shifts the blood glucose set point recognised by the beta cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glucokinase is not directly stimulated by fructose 2,6-bisphosphate; that molecule instead regulates phosphofructokinase-1, a later glycolytic enzyme, and (in its bisphosphatase-controlled balance) gluconeogenesis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Unlike hexokinase, which is inhibited by its own product glucose-6-phosphate, glucokinase is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, which is part of why it can keep operating even as glucose-6-phosphate accumulates in a well-fed liver.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Glucokinase's expression is restricted mainly to liver and pancreatic beta cells (unlike hexokinase, which is expressed in most tissues), not broadly expressed across many tissues.

questions.learning_objective: State that glucokinase's high Km, above fasting blood glucose, underlies its role as the liver/beta-cell glucose sensor.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: The Km is above the fasting concentration of glucose in the blood", p43

questions.title: Vigorously contracting muscle compared with the resting state
questions.question: Compared with the resting state, vigorously contracting skeletal muscle shows:

options.E: Increased reduction of pyruvate to lactate

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vigorous contraction increases, rather than decreases, glycolytic flux signals such as fructose 2,6-bisphosphate as the muscle ramps up glycolysis to meet its energy demand.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vigorous contraction raises, not lowers, the NADH/NAD+ ratio, since ATP demand outpaces the respiratory chain's capacity to reoxidise NADH under these conditions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vigorous contraction typically outpaces local oxygen delivery, producing relative hypoxia within the working muscle, not increased oxygen availability.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vigorous contraction increases, not decreases, the AMP/ATP ratio, as ATP is consumed faster than it can be regenerated, which is itself a signal that activates glycolysis.
explanations.E: Correct. During vigorous contraction, ATP demand rises faster than the respiratory chain can reoxidise NADH, so the NADH/NAD+ ratio climbs. This drives an increased reduction of pyruvate to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, which regenerates the NAD+ glycolysis needs to keep running (via glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase) even as oxygen delivery lags behind demand. This shift toward lactate production is the muscle's way of sustaining rapid ATP generation from glycolysis under exactly these conditions.

questions.title: Route of liver glucose uptake
questions.question: Glucose uptake by:

options.A: Brain cells is through energy-requiring (active) transport
options.B: Liver cells is through facilitated diffusion involving a glucose transporter
options.D: Most cells is through simple diffusion up a concentration gradient

explanations.A: Incorrect. Brain cells take up glucose by facilitated diffusion (via GLUT-1/GLUT-3), not by energy-requiring active transport.
explanations.B: Correct. Liver cells take up glucose via GLUT-2, a high-capacity, high-Km facilitated-diffusion glucose transporter that does not require insulin or energy input, allowing glucose to move down its concentration gradient into hepatocytes. This insulin-independent, bidirectional facilitated-diffusion route is what lets the liver both take up glucose after a meal and export glucose (from glycogenolysis or gluconeogenesis) between meals through the same transporter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Intestinal mucosal cells take up dietary glucose mainly via SGLT-1, a sodium-coupled secondary active transporter, not a process that itself requires insulin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Most cells take up glucose by carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion (via a GLUT transporter), not by simple diffusion, since glucose is too polar to cross the lipid bilayer unassisted.

questions.title: Substrate for aldolase
questions.question: The substrate for aldolase is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 1,3-diphosphoglycerate is a later glycolytic intermediate, downstream of aldolase's own reaction; it is not aldolase's substrate.
explanations.B: Correct. Aldolase splits fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (the product of phosphofructokinase-1's committed step) into two three-carbon fragments, dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. This is the pathway's central bond-cleaving step, converting a single six-carbon sugar phosphate into two molecules that continue through the remaining, energy-yielding half of glycolysis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glucose-6-phosphate is an early glycolytic intermediate, upstream of aldolase's own reaction; it is not aldolase's substrate.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fructose-6-phosphate is aldolase's substrate's own immediate precursor (before phosphofructokinase-1 acts on it), not the substrate aldolase itself acts on.

questions.title: Source of energy for muscle contraction in anaerobic glycolysis
questions.question: Available energy for muscle contraction is obtained during anaerobic glycolysis from which of the following?

options.B: The reduction of pyruvate to lactate
options.C: The formation of fructose 1,6-diphosphate from fructose-6-phosphate

explanations.A: Correct. The conversion of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 3-phosphoglycerate, catalysed by phosphoglycerate kinase, is one of glycolysis's two substrate-level phosphorylation steps, directly generating ATP from a high-energy phosphate bond without needing the respiratory chain or oxygen. Because this ATP-generating step does not require oxygen, it is exactly the kind of reaction that supplies usable energy for muscle contraction under anaerobic conditions. This, together with the later pyruvate kinase reaction, is where anaerobic glycolysis's net ATP yield actually comes from.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The reduction of pyruvate to lactate does not itself generate ATP; its purpose is to regenerate NAD+ so that glycolysis's earlier, ATP-generating steps can keep running.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The formation of fructose 1,6-bisphosphate from fructose-6-phosphate, catalysed by phosphofructokinase-1, consumes an ATP rather than producing one; it is part of glycolysis's energy-investment phase, not its energy payoff.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The conversion of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, catalysed by GAPDH, generates NADH (and sets up the next step's ATP yield) but does not itself directly generate ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation.

questions.title: The amphibolic pathway
questions.question: An amphibolic pathway among the following is:

explanations.A: Correct. The citric acid cycle is described as amphibolic because it serves both catabolic and anabolic roles at once: it oxidises acetyl-CoA for energy, but its intermediates are also continuously drawn off to build haem, several amino acids, fatty acids and (via oxaloacetate) glucose. This dual catabolic-and-anabolic character, rather than a purely one-directional role, is exactly what the term "amphibolic" describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The HMP (pentose phosphate) shunt is primarily anabolic/reductive in character (generating NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate), not classically described as amphibolic.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glycolysis is primarily catabolic, breaking down glucose for energy and pyruvate; it is not classically described as amphibolic in the way the citric acid cycle is.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gluconeogenesis is primarily anabolic, building glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors; it is not classically described as amphibolic.

questions.title: Anaplerotic carboxylation reaction
questions.question: An anaplerotic reaction which sustains the availability of oxaloacetate is the carboxylation of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Citrate is a citric acid cycle intermediate formed from oxaloacetate condensing with acetyl-CoA; carboxylating citrate is not the anaplerotic reaction that replenishes oxaloacetate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Succinate is a citric acid cycle intermediate itself, downstream of oxaloacetate in the cycle; carboxylating succinate is not this anaplerotic reaction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glutamate can feed into the cycle via alpha-ketoglutarate through transamination or deamination, not through a carboxylation reaction that directly produces oxaloacetate.
explanations.D: Correct. Pyruvate carboxylase carboxylates pyruvate to oxaloacetate, using biotin as its coenzyme and ATP, in the citric acid cycle's key anaplerotic ("filling up") reaction. This reaction is especially important when cycle intermediates are being continuously drawn off for biosynthesis (the cycle's amphibolic role), since without replenishment the cycle would otherwise stall for lack of oxaloacetate to accept the next acetyl-CoA.

questions.title: Coenzymes required by PDH and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
questions.question: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex require the following for their oxidative decarboxylation:

explanations.A: Incorrect. NAD+ and FAD alone are not sufficient; these two complexes' oxidative decarboxylation reactions require a total of five coenzymes/cofactors.
explanations.B: Correct. Both pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are large multi-enzyme complexes that require the same set of five coenzymes for their oxidative decarboxylation reactions: thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), lipoic acid (lipoate), coenzyme A (CoASH), FAD and NAD+. explanations.C: Incorrect. CoASH and lipoic acid alone omit TPP, FAD and NAD+, all of which are also required.
explanations.D: Incorrect. CoASH and TPP alone omit lipoate, FAD and NAD+, all of which are also required.

questions.title: What the citric acid cycle regenerates to stay continuous
questions.question: Tricarboxylic acid cycle to be continuous requires the regeneration of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Alpha-oxoglutaric acid (alpha-ketoglutarate) is an intermediate produced and consumed within a single turn of the cycle; it is not the specific intermediate whose ongoing regeneration is what makes the cycle continuous.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pyruvic acid is not itself a citric acid cycle intermediate; it enters the cycle only indirectly, after conversion to acetyl-CoA.
explanations.C: Correct. The citric acid cycle is cyclic specifically because oxaloacetate, consumed when it condenses with acetyl-CoA to form citrate at the start of each turn, is regenerated at the end of that same turn. explanations.D: Incorrect. Malic acid (malate) is an intermediate within the cycle, converted to oxaloacetate near the cycle's end, but it is oxaloacetate itself, not malate, whose regeneration is the specific fact this question is testing.

questions.title: Hydrogen carrier for succinate to fumarate dehydrogenation
questions.question: Dehydrogenation of succinic acid to fumaric acid requires the following hydrogen carrier:

explanations.A: Incorrect. NADP+ is used mainly in reductive biosynthetic (anabolic) pathways such as fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis, not in this citric acid cycle dehydrogenation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glutathione is primarily an antioxidant/redox-buffering molecule, not the hydrogen carrier for succinate dehydrogenase's reaction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. NAD+ is the hydrogen carrier used by most other citric acid cycle dehydrogenases (isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, malate dehydrogenase), but not by succinate dehydrogenase specifically.
explanations.D: Correct. Succinate dehydrogenase, the enzyme that dehydrogenates succinate to fumarate, is the one citric acid cycle enzyme that is itself embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane as complex II of the respiratory chain, and it uses a flavoprotein (FAD, tightly enzyme-bound) as its hydrogen carrier rather than NAD+. questions.title: Biotin deficiency blocks pyruvate carboxylase
questions.question: A bodybuilder eats only egg whites for weeks to maximise protein intake, becomes hypoglycaemic, and is found to have a functional biotin deficiency. Which of the following enzymes is unable to catalyze a key step in synthesizing glucose from pyruvate?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glucose 6-phosphatase catalyses gluconeogenesis's final step and does not require biotin as a cofactor.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase does not require biotin either; it is a simple hydrolytic step, not a carboxylation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase decarboxylates oxaloacetate to PEP and does not use biotin as its cofactor.
explanations.D: Correct. Pyruvate carboxylase, the first committed step of gluconeogenesis from pyruvate, carboxylates pyruvate to oxaloacetate and specifically requires biotin as its cofactor; raw egg whites contain avidin, which binds biotin and prevents its absorption, so a diet of egg whites alone can precipitate a functional biotin deficiency that stalls exactly this step and impairs gluconeogenesis, producing hypoglycaemia. Cooking the egg whites denatures avidin and removes this risk, which is why the deficiency is specifically associated with RAW egg white consumption. This same biotin dependence is shared by acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the analogous committed step of fatty acid synthesis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Phosphoglycerate kinase is a glycolytic (and gluconeogenic, in reverse) enzyme that does not use biotin; it catalyses a simple phosphate transfer, not a carboxylation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify pyruvate carboxylase as the biotin-dependent enzyme of gluconeogenesis blocked by biotin deficiency.

questions.title: Von Gierke's disease is glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency
questions.question: Glucose-6-phosphatase is absent or deficient in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. McArdle's disease (type V) is caused by muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency, not glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cori's disease (type III) is caused by debranching enzyme deficiency, a different enzyme acting earlier in glycogenolysis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pompe's disease (type II) is caused by lysosomal acid maltase (alpha-glucosidase) deficiency, an entirely different, lysosomal storage mechanism.
explanations.D: Correct. Von Gierke's disease (type I glycogen storage disease) is caused by deficiency of glucose 6-phosphatase, the enzyme that dephosphorylates glucose 6-phosphate to free glucose at the final common step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; its absence produces severe fasting hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia and hepatomegaly with a fatty liver. Because glucose 6-phosphate cannot exit the pathway as free glucose, it instead backs up into glycolysis (raising lactate) and the pentose phosphate pathway (raising purine synthesis and hence uric acid). This distinctive four-feature picture -- hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia and hyperlipidaemia -- is what points specifically to the phosphatase step rather than to phosphorylase or debranching enzyme.

questions.title: Glycogen phosphorylase releases glucose-1-phosphate
questions.question: Glycogen is converted to glucose-1-phosphate by:

explanations.A: Correct. This tissue difference in downstream fate is the direct consequence of what phosphorylase itself produces at this first step.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Branching enzyme acts during glycogen synthesis, creating the alpha-1,6 branch points; it plays no role in releasing glucose 1-phosphate from glycogen.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Phosphatase (specifically glucose 6-phosphatase, in the liver) acts later in the pathway, dephosphorylating glucose 6-phosphate to free glucose; it does not act on glycogen itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. UDPG (UDP-glucose) transferase (glycogen synthase) works in the synthesis direction, adding glucose units onto glycogen from UDP-glucose, the opposite of breaking glycogen down.

questions.title: A 2-hour OGTT of 210 mg/dL diagnoses diabetes
questions.question: A 33-year-old obese man with a strong family history of type 2 diabetes undergoes laboratory testing to evaluate his risk. Which of the following results would lead to a diagnosis of diabetes?

options.A: A single fasting blood glucose level of 160 mg/dL
options.B: The presence of a reducing sugar in his urine
options.C: A 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test with a blood glucose level of 210 mg/dL
options.D: A single fasting blood glucose level of 110 mg/dL
options.E: A single random glucose level of 190 mg/dL

explanations.A: Incorrect. While a fasting glucose that high would in fact be diagnostic in its own right on standard criteria, the option written here is not the one the printed key selects as correct in this bank; the OGTT result is the more clearly definitive standard test named.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A reducing substance in urine is a non-specific screening finding (and can occur in other conditions) rather than a definitive diagnostic criterion for diabetes.
explanations.C: Correct. A 2-hour value of 200 mg/dL or higher on a standard oral glucose tolerance test is one of the accepted diagnostic thresholds for diabetes mellitus, and 210 mg/dL clears that threshold; the OGTT is a standard, reproducible diagnostic test precisely because it standardises the glucose challenge and the timing of the sample. It remains the reference test used when fasting or random values are borderline or ambiguous. This vignette's obese patient with a strong family history is exactly the clinical picture in which an OGTT is typically ordered to confirm or exclude a diagnosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A fasting glucose of 110 mg/dL falls in the pre-diabetic (impaired fasting glucose) range, below the fasting threshold of 126 mg/dL required for a diabetes diagnosis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A random glucose of 190 mg/dL is below the 200 mg/dL threshold used for a random-glucose-based diagnosis (and would also need to be paired with symptoms), so it does not by itself meet diagnostic criteria the way the OGTT result does.

questions.learning_objective: Apply the OGTT diagnostic threshold (2-hour glucose >= 200 mg/dL) to diagnose diabetes.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: A 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test with a blood glucose level of 210 mg/dL", p98

questions.title: Serum C-peptide is undetectable in type 1 diabetes
questions.question: Serum C-peptide is not detectable in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gestational diabetes involves relative insulin resistance during pregnancy; the pancreas still produces insulin (and C-peptide), which remains detectable.
explanations.B: Correct. Type 1 diabetes follows autoimmune destruction of the pancreatic beta cells, making the deficiency of insulin absolute; because C-peptide is co-secreted with endogenous insulin from the same proinsulin precursor, and the beta cells that would make it no longer exist, C-peptide becomes essentially undetectable. This distinction also makes C-peptide clinically useful for telling type 1 from type 2 diabetes and for distinguishing endogenous insulin production from injected insulin, which carries no C-peptide at all. A patient on insulin therapy whose own C-peptide remains detectable therefore still has functioning beta cells, pointing toward type 2 rather than type 1 disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Renal diabetes" (renal glycosuria) is a defect of renal glucose reabsorption, not a beta-cell or insulin-secretion disorder; C-peptide remains detectable.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Type 2 diabetes is insulin resistance with only a relative and progressive secretory failure, so the beta cells that remain still produce measurable, if reduced, C-peptide, unlike the essentially complete absence seen in type 1.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that C-peptide is undetectable in type 1 diabetes because beta-cell destruction makes insulin deficiency absolute.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Type 1 diabetes", p99

questions.title: HDL transports cholesterol from extrahepatic tissues to the liver
questions.question: Cholesterol is transported from extrahepatic tissues to the liver by which of the following lipoproteins?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chylomicrons carry dietary lipid, mainly triacylglycerol, from the intestine outward to peripheral tissues; they do not carry cholesterol back to the liver from the periphery.
explanations.B: Correct. HDL is the lipoprotein responsible for reverse cholesterol transport, carrying excess cholesterol from peripheral (extrahepatic) tissues back to the liver for excretion or reuse -- the reason it is called the "good" cholesterol, in contrast to LDL, which delivers cholesterol outward to tissues. HDL is the smallest and densest of the major lipoproteins, with the highest protein content of the series, which fits its role of ferrying cholesterol rather than bulk delivering it. A higher HDL level is generally protective against atherosclerosis precisely because of this cholesterol-clearing function.
explanations.C: Incorrect. VLDL, made by the liver, carries hepatic triacylglycerol outward to peripheral tissues; it is not the vehicle for returning cholesterol to the liver.
explanations.D: Incorrect. LDL delivers cholesterol to peripheral tissues (the outward direction), the opposite of the extrahepatic-to-liver transport this question asks about.

questions.learning_objective: State that HDL carries out reverse cholesterol transport from extrahepatic tissues to the liver.

questions.title: Chylomicrons contain mainly dietary triacylglycerol
questions.question: Which of the following statements about circulating lipoproteins is correct?

options.A: Chylomicrons release cholesterol to adipose tissues
options.B: VLDL releases cholesterol to the liver
options.C: LDL contains mainly dietary triacylglycerol in its core
options.D: Chylomicrons contain mainly dietary triacylglycerol in their core

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chylomicrons deliver triacylglycerol (via lipoprotein lipase) to adipose and muscle tissue, not cholesterol specifically as their main cargo delivered to fat.
explanations.B: Incorrect. VLDL is made by the liver to export hepatic triacylglycerol outward to tissues; it does not release cholesterol to the liver, which is HDL's job.
explanations.C: Incorrect. LDL's core is mainly cholesteryl ester, not dietary triacylglycerol; dietary triacylglycerol is chylomicrons' cargo, not LDL's.
explanations.D: Correct. Chylomicrons, assembled in intestinal epithelial cells from dietary lipid, are about 98% lipid by mass and carry mainly dietary triacylglycerol in their core, which lipoprotein lipase then hydrolyses at capillary beds to deliver fatty acids to adipose and muscle tissue. Chylomicrons are accordingly the largest and least dense of the major lipoproteins, carrying the least protein of the series, consistent with their role as bulk triacylglycerol carriers rather than as regulatory or cholesterol-shuttling particles. Their remnant particles, after most of the triacylglycerol is removed, are then cleared by the liver.

questions.title: Chylomicrons are packaged in intestinal epithelial cells
questions.question: A 16-year-old female with a rare genetic deficiency of lipoprotein lipase is found to have abnormally elevated chylomicrons in her serum (type 1 hyperlipidaemia). In what type of cell are triacylglycerols packaged into chylomicrons in the first place?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Heart cells consume fatty acids for energy; they do not assemble chylomicrons.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The liver assembles VLDL, not chylomicrons, from its own (not dietary) triacylglycerol.
explanations.C: Correct. Dietary triacylglycerol, absorbed as monoglycerides and fatty acids, is re-esterified and packaged into chylomicrons specifically within intestinal epithelial (mucosal) cells, which then secrete the chylomicrons into intestinal lymphatics for eventual entry into the bloodstream; a downstream defect in lipoprotein lipase, as in this vignette, does not change where chylomicrons are made, only how efficiently their triacylglycerol is later cleared from the circulation. This is why a patient with lipoprotein lipase deficiency still produces chylomicrons normally but cannot clear them from the plasma, leading to their marked accumulation and the resulting type 1 hyperlipidaemia. The assembly step and the clearance step are therefore two separate points in the pathway that a single question can probe independently.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adipose cells store triacylglycerol delivered to them by chylomicrons and VLDL; they do not assemble chylomicrons themselves.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Muscle cells take up and oxidise fatty acids delivered by lipoprotein lipase; they play no role in chylomicron assembly.

questions.learning_objective: State that chylomicrons are assembled and packaged in intestinal epithelial cells.

questions.title: Carnitine transports long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria
questions.question: Transport of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for beta-oxidation needs which of the following molecules?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Creatine phosphate is an energy-buffering molecule in muscle, unrelated to mitochondrial fatty acid transport.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Creatinine is a waste product of creatine metabolism, cleared by the kidney; it has no role in fatty acid transport.
explanations.C: Correct. A long-chain fatty acid is first activated to fatty acyl-CoA in the cytosol, but the inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to acyl-CoA itself; carnitine is the shuttle molecule that carries the fatty acyl group across, via carnitine acyltransferase I (outer membrane) and II (inner membrane), the rate-limiting and hormonally regulated step of beta-oxidation. Malonyl-CoA, the first intermediate of fatty acid synthesis, inhibits carnitine acyltransferase I, which is how the cell prevents newly synthesised fatty acids from being immediately oxidised again. Short- and medium-chain fatty acids, unlike long-chain ones, can cross the mitochondrial membrane without this carnitine shuttle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Creatine (as opposed to carnitine) is part of the phosphocreatine energy buffer system in muscle, not the fatty acid transport shuttle.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Beta carotene is a vitamin A precursor with no role in mitochondrial fatty acid transport.

questions.learning_objective: State that carnitine transports long-chain fatty acyl groups into mitochondria for beta-oxidation.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Carnitine", p130

questions.title: Fatty acid activation for beta-oxidation occurs in the cytoplasm
questions.question: Which of the following is a site of fatty acid activation for beta-oxidation?

explanations.A: Correct. A fatty acid is activated to its CoA thioester (fatty acyl-CoA) in the cytoplasm (cytosol), consuming ATP; only after this activation step, and only after carnitine shuttles the acyl group across the mitochondrial membrane, does beta-oxidation itself proceed inside the mitochondrial matrix. Activation effectively spends the equivalent of two ATP per fatty acid, a cost subtracted when calculating the pathway's net ATP yield. Keeping the sequence straight -- cytoplasmic activation, then carnitine-mediated transport, then mitochondrial oxidation -- is what a stem naming a specific compartment is testing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The plasma membrane is not the site of fatty acid activation; that reaction occurs in the cytosol using the enzyme acyl-CoA synthetase (thiokinase).
explanations.C: Incorrect. The endoplasmic reticulum has its own separate long-chain fatty acid activation activity for lipid synthesis, but is not the site named for beta-oxidation's own activation step.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The Golgi apparatus is involved in protein/lipid trafficking and modification, not fatty acid activation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The mitochondria is where beta-oxidation itself (the repeated cycles of oxidation) occurs, after activation and carnitine transport, not where activation happens; activation is a cytoplasmic step.

questions.learning_objective: State that fatty acid activation for beta-oxidation occurs in the cytoplasm, before carnitine-mediated mitochondrial entry.

questions.title: Complete oxidation of palmitic acid yields 129 ATP
questions.question: Complete oxidation of one molecule of palmitic acid (16 carbons) produces a number of ATP molecules equal to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 55 undercounts the total substantially, missing most of the ATP generated across beta-oxidation's seven cycles and the citric acid cycle turns that follow.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 138 overcounts; it does not subtract the two ATP equivalents spent activating the fatty acid to palmitoyl-CoA before oxidation begins.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 146 also overcounts, for the same reason (failing to subtract the activation cost).
explanations.D: Correct. Palmitic acid (16 carbons) undergoes seven cycles of beta-oxidation, each removing two carbons and yielding one FADH2 and one NADH, producing eight acetyl-CoA units in total; running the resulting FADH2, NADH and acetyl-CoA (each acetyl-CoA yielding further ATP through the citric acid cycle and respiratory chain) through standard ATP-yield accounting gives 131 gross ATP, minus the 2 ATP-equivalents spent activating the fatty acid at the start, for a net of 129 ATP. This net figure is what makes fat such an energy-dense fuel compared with glucose, whose complete oxidation yields only around 30-32 ATP per molecule. The exact number examiners expect can vary slightly by textbook convention, but 129 is the value this bank's printed key uses.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 89 undercounts, well below the correct net yield for a 16-carbon fatty acid's complete oxidation.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: 129", p131

questions.title: Water is not generated during each fatty acid oxidation cycle
questions.question: During each cycle of ongoing fatty acid oxidation, all of the following compounds are generated EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS generated each cycle, not the exception). Each turn of beta-oxidation removes two carbons and releases one acetyl-CoA.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS generated each cycle). Each cycle's dehydrogenation steps produce one NADH (and one FADH2) per turn.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS generated each cycle). Each turn regenerates a fatty acyl-CoA two carbons shorter than the one that entered it, which is what allows the cycle to repeat.
explanations.D: Correct -- this is the exception. Beta-oxidation itself does not directly generate water in its four repeating steps (dehydrogenation, hydration, oxidation, thiolytic cleavage); if anything, water is CONSUMED at the hydration step, not produced, and any water associated with the pathway overall is generated later, at the very end of the respiratory chain when oxygen is finally reduced. Confusing the cycle's own four steps with the downstream respiratory-chain consequences of the NADH and FADH2 it produces is the trap this stem is built to catch. Acetyl-CoA, NADH and a shortened fatty acyl-CoA are the three genuine products of each turn; water is not.

questions.learning_objective: Identify water as the product NOT directly generated in each beta-oxidation cycle.

questions.title: Beta-oxidation uses FAD and NAD+ as coenzymes
questions.question: In beta-oxidation of fatty acids, which of the following are utilized as coenzymes?

explanations.A: Incorrect. NADP+ is used in reductive biosynthetic pathways (such as fatty acid synthesis), not as a coenzyme accepting electrons during oxidative beta-oxidation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. FMN is a respiratory-chain (complex I) cofactor, not one of beta-oxidation's own two coenzymes; beta-oxidation instead pairs FAD with NAD+.
explanations.C: Incorrect. FADH2 and NADH are the REDUCED products of the reaction, not the oxidized coenzyme forms consumed at the start of each cycle; the coenzymes utilised (accepting electrons) are FAD and NAD+.
explanations.D: Correct. Each turn of beta-oxidation uses FAD as the coenzyme for its first (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase) oxidation step and NAD+ as the coenzyme for its third (3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase) oxidation step, generating FADH2 and NADH respectively, which then feed electrons into the respiratory chain at complex II and complex I. This is the mirror image of fatty acid synthesis, which instead spends NADPH as its reducing power, a deliberate separation that lets the cell run oxidation and synthesis at the same time without one pathway short-circuiting the other. Recognising FAD-then-NAD+ as beta-oxidation's own coenzyme pair is a reliable way to answer this kind of question quickly.

questions.learning_objective: State that beta-oxidation uses FAD and NAD+ (not NADP+ or FMN) as its coenzymes.

questions.title: Nicotinic acid is not a lipolytic hormone
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a lipolytic hormone?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS lipolytic, not the exception). Thyroxine activates protein kinase A directly, promoting hormone-sensitive lipase activity and lipolysis.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS lipolytic). Glucagon raises cAMP via adenylyl cyclase, activating protein kinase A and hormone-sensitive lipase, driving lipolysis.
explanations.C: Correct -- this is the exception (NOT lipolytic). Nicotinic acid (niacin, at pharmacological doses) is used clinically as an anti-lipolytic (lipid-lowering) agent: it lowers cAMP and suppresses hormone-sensitive lipase activity, reducing free fatty acid release from adipocytes, the opposite of what the other three hormones in this list do. This anti-lipolytic action is why high-dose niacin has historically been used to lower plasma triglycerides and LDL cholesterol. explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS lipolytic). Epinephrine, like glucagon, raises cAMP via adenylyl cyclase and activates hormone-sensitive lipase, driving lipolysis as part of the fight-or-flight response.

questions.question: Hormone-sensitive lipase can hydrolyze the triacylglycerols inside which of the following?

questions.title: cAMP-activated triglyceride lipase regulates lipolysis
questions.question: Which of the following regulates lipolysis in adipocytes?

options.A: Activation of triglyceride lipase as a result of hormone-stimulated increases in cAMP levels
options.B: Activation of fatty acid synthesis mediated by cAMP
options.C: Glycerol phosphorylation to prevent futile esterification of fatty acids
options.D: Activation of cAMP production by insulin

explanations.A: Correct. Lipolytic hormones (glucagon, epinephrine, and others) raise intracellular cAMP via adenylyl cyclase; cAMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates and activates hormone-sensitive (triglyceride) lipase, the step that directly controls the rate of lipolysis in adipocytes. Insulin reverses this entire cascade, lowering cAMP (via phosphodiesterase activation) and activating a phosphatase that dephosphorylates and inactivates the lipase, which is why insulin is the body's principal anti-lipolytic signal. This cAMP-PKA-lipase axis is therefore the single regulatory node that lipolytic and anti-lipolytic signals both act through, in opposite directions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. cAMP inhibits, rather than activates, fatty acid synthesis (by inactivating acetyl-CoA carboxylase); it does not mediate lipogenesis activation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Adipose tissue lacks glycerol kinase, so it cannot phosphorylate the glycerol released by lipolysis at all, let alone use that as the regulatory step controlling lipolysis; this is a distractor built on an unrelated fact about adipose glycerol handling.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Insulin lowers, rather than raises, cAMP (by activating phosphodiesterase), which is exactly why insulin is anti-lipolytic rather than a driver of lipolysis.

questions.learning_objective: State that lipolytic hormones activate hormone-sensitive (triglyceride) lipase via cAMP and protein kinase A.
